speechtext: Tariff Board Report on Textiles changers, about a week ago, I can assure the house that the board's recommendations contained in the present report will receive most careful consideration by the government. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: TEXTILES
subsubtopic: REPORT ON REFERENCE NO. 125
speechtext: I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether you would not clarify our understanding of the rules and procedure in the house in connection with the statement just made by the minister. There seems to be growing up here a practice of reading lengthy statements arising out of reports from boards or commissions. This was not a ministerial statement. A ministerial statement is one which any member of the government has, of course, the right to make and on which we from time to time have the right to comment. But this was a summary of what is contained in the report on a textile reference sent to the board, and in that respect I think it is objectionable. I ask Your Honour for a ruling on the matter so that we may know how to proceed in the future.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TEXTILES
subsubtopic: REPORT ON REFERENCE NO. 125
speechtext:
Does any member wish to comment on the point raised by the hon. member for Laurier?
Mr. Fleming (Eglinlon: May I say this on the point raised by the hon. gentleman. He says that a practice is growing up. I think he has overlooked the fact that in this respect I have simply inherited and carried on a practice that was established before me. If the house does not wish these statements on tariff board references, believe me I shall be only too happy to be relieved of any necessity for stating to the house the gist of these reports. I understand these reports have been regarded by the house as having some value, and it has been the practice to give the house the gist or summary in brief form, as I have done today, of the reports. But if the house does not want these reports brought to the house, believe me I shall be only too happy to be relieved of this responsibility. However, I hope there will not be complaints afterwards about these matters not being brought to the attention of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: TEXTILES
subsubtopic: REPORT ON REFERENCE NO. 125
speechtext:
May I just add this word in connection with what the minister has said concerning the practice that developed earlier, when we were on the other side of the house. I can speak only for myself, of course; but I know that on no occasion when I tabled a report did I do other than table the report without any comment on it. I

doubt very much whether any of my colleagues who were in the government then did otherwise. In that respect I think the minister is in error. In any event, in the statement he has made the minister has by inference recognized the fact that the practice he has established is contrary to the rules.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TEXTILES
subsubtopic: REPORT ON REFERENCE NO. 125
speechtext: Just to clarify the point, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I was not referring to the practice established by the hon. gentleman. I was referring to the practice established by my predecessors in relation to tariff board reports.

subtopic: TEXTILES
subsubtopic: REPORT ON REFERENCE NO. 125
speechtext: On that point may I just say this. Your Honour can look up the precedents and the facts, but I think you will find that in respect of reports of the tariff board which were tabled and which involved recommendations and policy decisions, perhaps short ministerial statements were made; but with regard to reports tabled which did not have those consequences, statements were not made.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TEXTILES
subsubtopic: REPORT ON REFERENCE NO. 125
speechtext:
There may perhaps be some difficulty from time to time in determining what matters contained in a report should be brought to the attention of parliament. It is perhaps not an easy decision for a minister to make, because he may feel that if he does not bring the matter before the house, complaint may be made on that score. But I think it should be fairly easy to determine what are matters of policy to be announced, and what are documents of another kind which need no explanation. It seems to me that a report by a board which is tabled stands on its own feet, and if no policy is being announced it should not take up the time of the house on routine proceedings.
I am not saying that the minister was not justified in thinking that he was acting in accordance with the previous practice, but I do say that the house should be jealous of its use of this time. It should not be used for the making of statements which are not of immediate importance by reason of the fact that they announce important policy or something of urgent public interest, nor for the asking of questions which are not within the customary limits.
It is my own view that statements should be introduced sparingly, that they should be of importance and should contain some decision of the government which it wishes to announce.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISALLOWANCE OF LABOUR LEGISLATION
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister say whether the government has under consideration the disallowance of the controversial labour legislation passed by the government of Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISALLOWANCE OF LABOUR LEGISLATION
speechtext: I think, as a question of order, that we dealt with that matter during the last session. It is irregular for inquiry to be made of the government with respect to disallowance until after the period for disallowance has expired.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISALLOWANCE OF LABOUR LEGISLATION
speechtext: On the point of order you have raised, Mr. Speaker, I think that if you refer to Hansard of last year you will find that this question was raised on a number of occasions and that an answer was given. It was ruled, however, that in a general debate we could not speak at length on this particular point. But the question was raised-and I could quote chapter and verse-as to whether the matter was still under consideration and when the government would come to a decision. Since the government has only till about March 6 in which to reach a decision, I think it is in order to ask whether or not this matter is still under consideration and when a decision may be made.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISALLOWANCE OF LABOUR LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I should like that question to stand because I am quite clearly of the view that it is not in order during the disallowance period for parliament to inquire into the exercise of the prerogative of disallowance. Perhaps I could give the hon. member the reference at the present time. I refer to citation 161 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition:
Disallowance of provincial laws is not one of the functions of the dominion parliament. The fact that this subject is dealt with in section 90 of the British North America Act and not in section 91 shows clearly that the legislator did not intend to include it with the residue of powers vested in the dominion parliament. The only authority that
388	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry can disallow provincial laws is the governor in council. As the governor in council is responsible to parliament, the House of Commons may criticize the action taken by the cabinet in cases of proposed disallowances, but a member cannot raise a debate on a provincial act on the motion to go into supply-
When the year within which disallowance may take place has expired, the government's action or inaction may be discussed in the House of Commons. The practice usually followed has been to wait until the question of disallowance has been decided upon by the government and then to move for the production of papers relating thereto.
I should think it would be in order to ask the government whether it had or had not disallowed the legislation, but not to discuss the matter.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATION TO EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the growing importance of the institutions of the communities and of our relations with these six-nation arrangements, the Canadian government has now decided to seek accreditation of our ambassador in Brussels as the Canadian representative to the three communities. The Canadian request was submitted some weeks ago, and in accordance with the usual procedure a formal reply is expected within the next few weeks. It was our intention to make a joint announcement in Ottawa and in Brussels when these procedures were completed.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether he proposes to proceed at this session of parliament with the proposal he made at a Conservative meeting in Ottawa on December 2 to the effect that a parliamentary committee should be set up, as reported in the press, to "comb through the laws and regulations of the land in search of provisions that contravene fundamental freedoms or deny equality under the law"?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE THIS SESSION TO SCRUTINIZE LAWS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman gave me no notice of this question, and of course he is not required to do so. I was referring in particular to those matters, and I am not going into them on the orders of the day, which shocked the conscience of Canadians during the period of time when the party opposite formed the government of the

Inquiries of the Ministry day. I felt and I still feel that one matter that might well be brought before the house would be the setting up of a committee similar to that in the British House of Commons known as the scrutiny committee. It would examine legislation being passed by parliament and already on the statute books, and would examine orders in council, which are not passed by parliament directly, to the end that anything in the nature of a contravention of fundamental freedoms would be brought to the attention of the house as a whole.
It has worked out very well in the United Kingdom, where it has brought about the removal and excision from various orders in council of sections which otherwise would have remained in effect. It is an interparty group designed to make parliament more effective and more assuredly the custodian of the rights of the people. I am prepared to discuss that matter with the hon. gentleman if it appeals to him, because naturally it would require a degree of co-operation on the part of members of all parties in the house. Knowing his desire to make parliament more effective, I would think that an examination of the activities of that committee in the British House of Commons would commend itself to his attention. speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Emilien Morissette for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Argue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at ten o'clock last evening I was discussing the government's mixed up policy on North 79951-0-26i
The Address-Mr. Hellyer American air defence. I said that the government subscribed to the theory of defence in depth, but does not back its belief with action.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member might give a minute for the house to settle down so that we can hear his address.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Secretary Gates referred to the family of weapons, the mix. This includes the manned interceptor as the first line of defence, the Bomarc anti-aircraft missile as the second line or area defence, and the Nike as the third or spot defence.
The Bomarc is not a weapon by itself apart from its family. General Kuter explained the position clearly at the NATO parliamentary conference in Washington on Wednesday, November 18 last. In reply to a question by Senator Wylie of the United States, which I will quote, he said:
Senator Wylie: Is the Bomarc the answer to the bomber?
General Kuter:	No, sir. There is no single
answer to the bomber. The bomber or the air-to-surface missile requires now, will require as far into the future as I can see, the longer range aircraft to force the bomber to use his defence tactics or to employ his decoys to force him into effective methods of approach and tactics. The Bomarc follows closely behind that long-range fighter at very high kill capability, and requires behind it a more intensive defence of the local area. I believe we will always require the family of weapons that gives us all of those technical and tactical advantages.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the Bomarc is not a weapon to be used by itself.
Canada has no policy; we are half and half. We are neither in nor out. We are like a bather knee deep in frigid water who, fearing the depth, cannot decide whether to plunge in and swim to yonder shore or to beat a hasty retreat to the point of origin.
I have reread Hansard of February 23 last year, and I am saddened to learn that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) deceived the house and the Canadian people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Withdraw.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He clearly gave the impression that the Bomarc was a substitute for -

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is accusing the Prime Minister of misleading the people of Canada, and I ask that that remark be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: As I heard the hon. member, he did not say "misled" but "deceived". I think perhaps, on reflection, the hon. member would like to modify that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I did not say deliberately deceived. I do not say it was intentional, but "misled" is quite satisfactory

The Address-Mr. Hellyer as far as I am concerned. The Prime Minister clearly gave the impression that the Bomarc was a substitute for the manned interceptor rather than a complementary weapon. At page 1302 of Hansard for February 23 last, he is reported as saying:
On the other hand, we have available to us the Bomarc, whose area of defence and defensive action is not far removed from that of the CF-105, but the difference in expenditure has been clearly set out. The cost of the Bomarc missile to Canada, as compared to the $781 million of the CF-105, is approximately $110.8 million. That represents something that must be taken into consideration, all things being equal, and the defensive properties of each being about the same.
Well, all things are not equal, and this misleading impression was not just one which I alone obtained, it was taken up by a number of other people and quoted in an editorial in the Globe and Mail some time after the Prime Minister's statement. It is most unfortunate that he created this impression which is not in accordance with the facts.
A week ago last Monday he congratulated himself and his government for the decision taken last February to cancel the Avro Arrow. Yet at the same time the United States is asking us now to go ahead with the re-equipping of our air defence squadrons and accept United States aircraft not clearly comparable to the great Canadian plane which was cut up with acetylene torches.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: But the statement that the United States have asked Canada to do that is quite wrong, for it was an officer of the United States air force who raised the question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Minister of National Defence can make his speech later. He has just told us that the responsible officer of the United States air force, General Kuter, the
man who was in command of North American air defence, has asked that we replace this type of aircraft with supersonic aircraft. If that is not a request from the United States, what is?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is a field commander asking; not the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We are told that the matter of replacement for the CF-100 for home defence is under active consideration by the R.C.A.F. and by the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As soon as I have finished. Secretary Gates warns us that in the light of re-appraisal it may be necessary to put greater reliance on manned interceptors because of their greater flexibility.

It is not my intention to thresh old straw, but the Prime Minister made one other reference, to be found on page 14 of Hansard, which I should like to mention. He said the decision to cancel the Avro Arrow was not his but was a cabinet decision. There is no doubt that that is true in the technical sense under our system of cabinet responsibility, but it is also true that the Prime Minister did decide to cancel the Arrow on or before January 1, 1959, weeks before he had told the cabinet anything about it. Some weeks and a few million dollars later he let the cabinet and the country in on his secret. The Prime Minister does not need to be so modest in sharing the responsibility. Now, of course, he takes pride in the decision. I just wish to take this opportunity to record one dissenting voice.
Had the decision been taken in the fall of 1957 soon after the first Sputnik was placed in orbit, on the basis that further effort to defend this country against the manned bomber was futile, it would have been defensible. It must be assumed that in such an event the productive capacity would have been transferred to some new project. In February, 1959, however, with no alternative in sight and with no jobs available for the displaced workers, the decision fails on economic ground's alone. After taking into consideration the increased gross national product that would have been generated by continuing the program, the net cost to the Canadian taxpayers on current account would not have been too great. If one adds to the balance sheet the human capital which has been lost by Canada to the United States and the United Kingdom and the far-reaching effect on immigration of skilled people to this country the total loss to the Canadian nation is staggering.
Now, it is so much human suffering and dislocation passed under the bridge. Thousands of the unemployed are still walking the streets. To them, the callous way in which the decision was handled is still an awful reality. To others, more fortunate, it has become merely a distasteful memory. It still remains, however, for the government to tell us the policy behind the act. Have we given up the policy of defence in depth against manned bombers, or have we not? We cannot remain half and half. The government cannot fool the Canadian people on this one much longer. The Prime Minister will find that the Canadian people are quite competent to judge a government that works both sides of a street.
At the same time as he was quoting Mr. Khrushchev in defence of the decision he took a year ago the Prime Minister raised another

question. Mr. Khrushchev, according to the right hon. gentleman, told the supreme Soviet that surface vessels were no longer effective and that underseas craft would replace them in the Soviet strategy. A few breaths later the Prime Minister told us, with his usual self satisfaction, of Canada's continuing development of surface vessels. If Mr. Khrushchev has vindicated half of the governments half policy on air defence, has he challenged the policy on naval defence? We should be told by the government whether its policy is to continue to rely on surface vessels and aircraft or whether we intend to follow-at a respectable lag-the Russian lead, and rely on underseas craft.

On this subject, Admiral Jerauld Wright, retiring supreme allied commander (Atlantic), told the NATO parliamentary conference in Washington on November 18, 1959:
Our nuclear propelled submarines, the most promising of all anti-submarine weapons in the Atlantic, are available ... for the destruction of both guided missile submarines and submarines operating against our sea lines of communication.
Admiral Wright feels that the anti-submarine submarine is the most promising defensive weapon in this field. When you find Mr. Khrushchev and Admiral Wright agreeing on something which is out of step with Canadian policy, it may be time for an agonizing reappraisal.
One of the most important considerations of Canadian defence policy at the present time is the conversion, or the possibility of conversion, from conventional to atomic weapons. In the nuclear class, we have been ;old of the Bomarc ground to air missile, the Lacrosse ground to ground missile, the Sidewinder air to air missile and, indirectly, the possibility of small atomic bombs being carried by the F-104G. The way this information has come to light is regrettable. There has been no clear-cut statement of policy by the government at any time during the discussions. What information we have has been given piecemeal in divers ways at press conferences at airports and other places, interviews, passing references and by statements of United States officers. Parliament and the Canadian people are entitled to a forthright statement of the government's intention in respect to atomic weapons, both defensive and offensive.
Even more amazing, perhaps, than the lack of a policy is that the government should tell us that we have committed ourselves in advance, and spent money, many months before an agreement has been worked out with the United States with respect to custody and
The Address-Mr. Hellyer control. We were reassured last week that negotiations are presently under way with the United States government. But we were given the same information last February, almost a year ago. It might have been prudent to have completed the negotiations before committing ourselves to the use of any particular equipment.
The Bomarc is the only atomic weapon which, we have been told, will be used by us for North American defence. If the manned bomber is as obsolete as the Prime Minister says it is, we will probably not proceed with the installation. Of course, the government will have spent a great deal of the taxpayers' money and when the cancellation is finally made the money will have been spent uselessly.
As far as the atomic weapons to be used by our forces in Europe are concerned, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) stated that every effort should be made to have them, as well as all nuclear and other weapons, placed under NATO control. This is in line with the idea of unified command and complete integration of forces which is widely held by the military. It would eliminate the present cast system of first-class nations and second class nations. Paul Henri Spaak, secretary general of NATO, touched on the problem which affects standardization of weapons when he spoke to the NATO parliamentary conference in Washington. He said that France is forced to rediscover today what has been well known to others for ten years. Furthermore, the United States is not prepared to share with its friends secrets which are already well known to its enemies.
NATO control of atomic weapons would not mean the development of manufacturing facilities in other countries; quite the reverse might be true. If the necessary weapons were available to NATO forces it might mean the elimination of costly and wasteful duplication of effort along national lines. We do not underestimate the difficulty of achieving this solution. We believe, however, that it is both desirable and possible. The Prime Minister has indicated great confidence in Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). This is a worthy project to which he can bend his diplomatic ability.
The central theme of any Canadian defence policy is its relationship with its United States neighbour and with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The Prime Minister has said that our policy has been one of collective defence. We agree that everything possible must be done to keep the alliance intact and strong.

I am in no way a rabid militarist, but I am absolutely certain that it would be sheer madness for the western world to lessen the military effort before the situation is entirely changed.
(Text):
Those who propose a unilateral reduction in our effort say that we could divert the saving to foreign aid. Very few have mentioned what seems to me a more significant and sensible alternative. It is often spoken of in a different context but very seldom related to defence. We should increase our total production.
As Dr. John Galbraith says in his book, "The Affluent Society", there are several ways of doing this. The most obvious and, if I may say so, the most conservative approach is to use the resources at present available. We have in this country at the present time almost 700,000 persons drawing unemployment insurance. If even half of these people could be given gainful employment we would increase our annual output by over a billion dollars.
There would, of course, be several claims against the increase. These would come from the workers themselves, from the capital employed and from government. Government's share should be sufficient to expand greatly participation in projects designed to assist the less developed countries of the
The Address-Mr. Hellyer world, while at the same time the re-employed workers should enjoy a much higher standard of living than at present.
Last year in May when the estimates of the Department of Labour were under consideration I suggested that the government embark on a massive scheme of adult re-education and rehabilitation. The idea was warmly applauded by the government. Months have gone by and there is no indication that the government has acted boldly. This is one positive way that the government could greatly assist individual Canadians and subsequently provide itself with additional tax revenue for domestic and foreign aid purposes. Such a policy, to me, is far more sensible than a policy of retrenchment and retreat.
As I said earlier, it is not the intrinsic value of Canada's contribution which is of paramount importance, it is the example we set. The government must not reduce defence expenditures simply because it thinks it can get away with it and use the saving to bail itself out of its financial mess. I have said repeatedly that most of the major defence decisions taken by this government have been based more on fiscal than on military considerations. I regret that the press reports of the government's intentions support this opinion. It is not just the security of Canada which is at stake but because of our key position in the alliance it is the principle of collective security for the whole free world.
The tests of success in the performance of the duties of the government involve hard decisions. If they are to do their duty they must often swim against the tide of private feeling. The matter of defence and national survival is too urgent and overwhelming in its importance to be considered lightly.
There are a great many questions we shall ask, Mr. Speaker, when the special committee on defence expenditure is set up. It is important that we get the best value possible for the money being spent. To do so it will be necessary for the government to give us a great deal more information than they have previously. If the witnesses are allowed to answer questions forthrightly and with candour the committee can be of considerable benefit to parliament and the country.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Moris-sette) and the seconder (Mrs. Casselman) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Perhaps I can best sum up the opinion of the house when I report the words of one of our more senior members who said that after 20 years of experience he wished that he had made or could make a contribution such as both of these members produced in the debate. He went on to say that they indeed set an extremely high standard, one which it would be difficult for future sessions of the house to live up to. May I say to both of them, and I know the house will agree, that the often perfunctory remarks of congratulation which are made on these occasions are not made on this occasion but are offered with all sincerity because they acquitted themselves in a very excellent fashion.

I should like to say a word or two about the remarks of the gentleman who has just resumed his seat. However, as I propose to say something on defence perhaps I can reserve that until then. I was going to refer to him as the opposition defence authority but as he did not make a constructive or original statement throughout his entire address, with the exception of his reference to someone's book, he can only be put in the category of a critic.
Before referring to his remarks, however, I propose to try to say one or two things of a constructive nature and perhaps I can best start by saying to you, sir, how proud Canadians were of the representation you gave our country in your recent tour. I trust that as you made your journey you did not encounter the experience which I regrettably and unfortunately encountered during a shorter tour, that of visiting areas of Europe which had relatively little information on the Canadian people and the Canadian economy. I spent some time in the United Kingdom and I must say that I was particularly concerned with the attitude that existed there. Not only is very little known about Canada but I sensed a rather unusual feeling that there was little desire to learn very much about our country.
I was also somewhat alarmed at reading, in many instances, a rather antagonistic press and one which in describing the events of Her Majesty's visit to Canada, in the majority of instances in which there were many references, completely misrepresented what had taken place in Canada. In fact, after some seven weeks in the United Kingdom, what I was able to bring back in the way of press clippings of Canadian activities would not have done credit to the obituary column of one of our daily newspapers. However, I would not like you to give the impression that any of these people with whom we have close association were anything but hospitable to those of us who went over.
The relationship, in so far as our position in the commonwealth is concerned, remains extremely high. But what does concern me is the fact that, not only in Europe but also in the United States we must, not only as a government but as a people, make every effort to discourage any image of Canada which is only going to suggest that we have a vast wilderness and that all we can produce is cold weather, mounted policemen and ducks. I argue that if we are to reach into the markets of the world we must be able to show we are well equipped, we are well qualified and that we have all the facilities. I say that this attitude, perhaps

to a degree, is partly our own responsibility. I suggest that not only government bureaus, both in trade and commerce and our tourist bureaus, but in addition industry and the people associated with the vast press of Canada, should endeavour to improve what I call the Canadian image abroad.
I think, sir, that it anything is known about Canada it is certainly the vast resources which have played an important part and contributed so much to the Canadian economy. This is what I experienced in various sections of Europe and in particular when I discussed our problems with various securities' analysts in New York. They know something, of course, about the resource development that is taking place here. Because of this, I am going to make one or two suggestions to the house, asking as I do whether or not we fully appreciate the size of our own resources and the contribution that they make to Canada. I then would ask a further question as to whether or not, from an administrative standpoint, we have geared ourselves to service these resources in the most efficient manner possible.
The outstanding feature of our economy, I suggest, is that we have such large resources, and such large reserves, as to be almost unbelievable. These statistics may be of interest to the house. At 1958 rates of consumption the estimated reserves in energy would last us over 1,000 years. In so far as petroleum alone is concerned, it would last from 800 to 1,600 years, and coal in excess of 1,400 years.
Perhaps what is most significant, Mr. Speaker, is that Canada, with less than 1 per cent of the world's population owns about 15 per cent of the world's known resources of fossil fuels. With this background, I suggest to the house we should examine the system whereby we administer these resources in so far as the crown has any control over them.
We have already, in a past session, established a national energy board which deals with the different operational problems of these resources. But it is interesting to note that many of such resources, both in dollar value and in quality, have two departments dealing specifically with the problems of these resources. I am not suggesting in this day we establish a new ministry, but I am somewhat concerned with a situation which finds three departments directly concerned with one industry alone, namely trade and commerce, transport and mines. It does seem to me we could efficiently collectively group under one head in one department such a resource, with one senior administrator responsible for the over-all picture. They could,
The Address-Mr. A.R. Smith thereby, make a useful contribution to the government service as well as to the interests developing these resources.
I go on to make a second suggestion in this respect. From time to time this house is asked to consider problems dealing with resources development. Invariably these problems are referred to one of three committees. Again, I realize that this is hardly the time to introduce a suggestion for another standing committee, but I do ask you, Mr. Speaker, when we are considering future committees of this house or reorganizing them, to give some thought to a standing committee dealing with resources only. In this way we would have a well informed body of members in this house who would be able to deal adequately with many of the pressing problems concerning these resources. Perhaps I might be permitted to say that in my own city a short time ago a group of geologists and technicians were called together, geologists from all over the world, in what was known as an Arctic symposium. There came, from some 20-odd countries, great authorities who had some knowledge of the geology of the resources in the Arctic.
Perhaps what is significant is, first of all, that it is generally agreed that the Soviet has made greater advances in many of these fields, particularly in the north, than we have. The second significant fact is that the minister of northern affairs very rightly said we plan to double our own contribution, as a government, through the mines branch concerned with this particular field of research. I believe, therefore, that the remarks which I have made indicate that the question of planning for our resources development is one of some urgency.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) today and earlier in the debate made some reference to the possibility of the establishment of a house committee on rules. I am sure that this will meet with the approval of all sides of the house because there are problems here which were well illustrated today in the volume of time it took to conduct a small amount of business. I am going to make one or two suggestions which this committee, assuming it is appointed, might take under advisement. Perhaps I should first of all say, Mr. Speaker, that in these suggestions I intend or imply no disrespect to the chair. This house recognizes, sir, the great contribution which you make in administering * and looking after the business of this house, sometimes under difficult circumstances. My suggestions are rather intended to help the situation rather than confuse it.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would point out to you that from time to time we find

The Address-Mr. A.R. Smith it necessary to extend the working hours of the house. We invariably do this late in the season, when it is very warm, and we realize it is going to be quite late in midsummer before we will be going back to our constituencies. My first suggestion, which is perhaps not too palatable to some, is that we should immediately give consideration to the extension of the working hours of the House of Commons. We have come down here to work. I suggest that we should take advantage of every hour that we can to process the legislation in this house.
The second suggestion I make deals with the number of days which are allocated to this throne speech debate. I suggest that, even in recent years, we have cut oft a number of days available to it, and that the committee might consider a further reduction. The third suggestion which I make is on the debate on the resolution introducing a bill, is often duplicated in the three readings which follow. I would suggest to the committee that they examine the possibility of eliminating this repetition.
The fourth suggestion, which is perhaps equally important, deals with the point which was raised by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) today, and that is the question of lengthy statements which are given by ministers of the crown. My suggestion here, sir, is, would it not be acceptable to the committee, and perhaps the house, to have these statements placed on the record as an appendix to Hansard. Then, in turn, the relevant replies could be introduced at a time when the estimates were under consideration, depending upon the problem dealt with in the statement. If there were a question of urgency requiring an earlier reply, then this would be something upon which the chair could advise the house.
The fifth point that I make is the question of members' speeches. I am not thinking so much of the throne speech debate itself but rather of the speeches that we hear where repetition follows repetition dealing with the subject matter of a particular bill. I have been as guilty an offender as has any member of this house. It seems to me that here again we can shorten up the proceedings if a custom of the house were accepted whereby repetition was cut to a minimum.
One of the last suggestions I would make deals with our committee system. I think the committee on rules should examine the question of whether or not we get full value from our committee system. I would ask them to examine, first of all, the size of the committees and, second, to have some regard to whether or not departments, after

they have been examined, can make a report to the house on the suggestions or recommendations which have been made by the committee in the previous session. I cite as an example the Department of National Defence where the minister followed this practice and gave as examples references where the department had accepted many of the suggestions. I think the committees would operate more efficiently under such a reference and that they would be given encouragement to attack their work with greater enthusiasm.
My last suggestion with regard to house rules deals with the question of the customs of the house itself. From time to time, Mr. Speaker, you will rule us out of order on a particular matter. Many of the senior members of the house obviously know that they are out of order but on a great many occasions the members who have not had this lengthy experience will not be aware of the fact that they have actually offended a house rule or a house custom. I am therefore going to suggest that some of us should go back to school and that, under the very efficient Clerk of the house, we should assemble discussion groups so that we might become better informed of our own house rules. Under such a practice I suggest that endless delays resulting from ignorance of the rules at least would be reduced to a minimum.
Finally, I come to the most difficult period of the day for you, Mr. Speaker. I refer to the matter of determining the question of relevancy during the question period. In a legislative assembly of which I had the privilege of being a member there was a practice-and after all, practices differ from one legislative body to another-to the effect that where a question was asked by an individual member the Speaker of the house ruled that if the information could be obtained by picking up the telephone, especially where it concerned a junior official, he would not allow the question. I am not necessarily subscribing to this view here. I realize that there are circumstances under which it would not be acceptable. However, I suggest that this committee should strengthen your hand completely so that relevancy shall be uppermost in our minds when directing questions.
I have made nine suggestions in all and I have not in any way recommended for the committee's examination anything which would reduce constructive debate or discussion within the house. I have made the point that it is essential that we shorten the sessions for the members of the House of Commons. If we do not do this, it will eventually become a matter of time before it is necessary to recognize that this business of being a

member of the house is a full twelve months' function in Ottawa. If that is the case, our remuneration or our salary is going to have to be based on a twelve months' period and not as it was initially intended, namely on a period of a few months, from four to five. It is quite obvious that, as the sessions grow longer and as we are limited in the time during which we can go back and in some way supplement our income, it is ridiculous to think that the members can continue as they have been endeavouring to live, maintaining, as so many of them do, two homes, on their present income.
I now turn to the matter of defence on which I wish to say a few words. I am sure the house welcomes the establishment of a special committee or a committee which will deal with defence matters. The house will recall that some 18 months ago the standing committee on estimates examined the estimates of the Department of National Defence. I have endeavoured to ask myself how these committees will differ. First of all, the new committee will be somewhat smaller. I think this will increase the efficiency in carrying out its business. The problems which only the committee itself can determine is which of various witnesses it will call, for the committee will be master of its own rules.
The question of whether or not we shall enter into the realm of policy is not going to be a simple one to answer. The basic rule which we followed previously was that where an estimate for an expenditure was involved, the question of policy also became involved to some extent. But the procedure of the committee or whether we accomplish our business in one month or six months is not the important thing. The important thing is that each of us assuming the responsibility of being a member-if, of course, we are a member of that committee-must recognize that we have a responsibility not just to make political headlines, but to make a contribution in some way in examining the defence expenditures of government.
I am a little bit suspicious that perhaps this is not the purpose especially when we hear various opposition elements within the house and outside discuss Canada's defence policy as a whole. On the one hand, we hear those people who attempt to introduce the question of sovereignty as though it was something brand new to them. They have forgotten the element of co-operation between the various countries during the war when sovereignty was never questioned at all. Now when they are concerned with perhaps the element of co-operation that we have been extended and are extending ourselves to the United States, they cry that we are losing our sovereignty.
The Address-Mr. A.R. Smith
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all responsible members of this house that sovereignty is not the question today. It is a question of survival. I believe that we should not only co-operate to the extent that we have with the United States in the defence of this continent but that we should extend our co-operation even further. I believe that we should sit with them and determine how best we are able to provide the forms of defence best suited to our type of economy and our ability to pay for them. I think it is essential that we work out-as has been done by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) and his associates on several occasions-a common understanding. In this respect I think the present Minister of National Defence has done more than any other minister of national defence in the history of Canada.
We have one other criticism which is generally heard and this is by those who advise us that it is wrong to carry any nuclear equipment, in particular warheads, with which to equip any of our defence weapons in Canada. Surely these people must realize that until such time as total defence with a built-in inspection system is possible we must defend ourselves with the most modern weapons and equipment possible. In the event of an emergency, these people would be the same ones who would be criticizing us for not having adequate defence.
Speaking as we have been of the importance or the necessity of maintaining defence and working toward the total reduction in arms, complete disarmament, we must give every support that we can as a nation to this objective. We must also, in my opinion, however be ready to accept something less than that, if we are not able to achieve full disarmament. Steps to eliminate surprise attack swiftly would be a step in this direction. Believing as I do in the importance of working out a disarmament agreement, as I say, until that time comes it is essential for Canada to maintain its defences in the strongest position possible because, as the lesson has proved in the past, the deterrent is still the best defence that we know.
I should now like to say just a word or two about certain remarks of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). He talked about the Prime Minister first of all deceiving -then the record was changed to misleading -the house. This hon. gentleman had a responsible position in a former government as an associate minister of defence. On one occasion-I could quote many-he introduced his own remarks by talking about the unimpressive performance of the Prime Minister who took many press clippings and read reports of speeches made by the Leader of

The Address-Mr. A.R. Smith the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, we have a Hansard in this house. But there is no official record outside the house, and it was necessary to call the Leader of the Opposition to order and read back to him some of the inconsistent remarks he had made from time to time. Therefore I intend to refer back to July 3 of 1959, page 5460 of Hansard, when the hon. member for Trinity said this:
It is true that the F-104 used by the U.S.A.F. is not the Mark G contemplated for our air division but the G differs from the others mainly in electronic equipment, there being no change in the airframe or engine.
Just before that he had said:
We further understand that the fatality rate of F-104 planes and pilots in the U.S.A.F. is unusually high. The accident rate is about double that of other U.S.A.F. fighters.
All of us in this house have a responsibility not only to our own conscience but to the people of Canada as a whole. I suggest to the hon. member that when he endeavoured to create fear and alarm in the minds of the armed forces, in particular the air force, by suggesting that this plane was a killer without any reference to the obvious changes which were required in its superstructure. He was doing a disservice to the pilots who will be flying these planes. Surely the hon. member must know that in all of the nine marks of the Spitfire there were several alterations in order to improve its efficiency and safety, and the same can be said of all the 16 front line aircraft used in the last war. Any suggestion that this aircraft is not suited to the conditions for which it is required is an erroneous one, and I suggest that he has been misleading the house in this respect.
I think it is important when we speak of defence that we stop thinking of only one possible aggressor. There is only one aggressor now, the U.S.S.R. I recall visiting the United States not too long ago when a senior military figure in that country said to me that it was his guess that in a few years we might well be sitting with the Russian chief of staff planning how we are going to defeat another possible aggressor. I think it is interesting to note that at the United Nations this year Russia adopted a somewhat more conciliatory attitude, and I think we must recognize that their economic offensive today is far more serious than their military threat, because their economic front is here, and we must meet it today.
I also suggest that in making any assessment of where a potential aggressor lies we must look at a group of people to the east, 600 million strong and recognize that our defences must be in a position to meet all

potential aggressors, not just one, and I suggest that this, too, has been the defence policy of our government.
I would like to make a reference to the general economy of our country, and again make what I hope is a suggestion of a constructive nature. Those of us on this side of the house take some pride that we hear less today about the problems of tight money than we did some six months ago. No one denies that many of the small merchants, those people who must maintain inventories, have indeed had a difficult period. But what is interesting is that the economy has advanced. My own city has expanded in every area possible. In fact, we have never had it so good in spite of a setback in one important industry. The gross national product of Canada is up 3 per cent. Housing starts are up 35 per cent, and so the record goes. Yet the opposition critics, prior to the opening of the house, appeared through every news media to criticize the monetary policies of this government, and then suddenly they stopped or, at least, altered their direction of attack. I think it was particularly significant that they altered their attack about the same time that an hon. senator of the Liberal party wrote a letter, as I understand it, to one of the Ottawa dailies congratulating the government on their monetary policies.
It is significant to note, I suggest, that following this every major bank president, and also the governor of the Bank of Canada, supported the principles, the actions which the Bank of Canada had taken with respect to credit. No one will at any time discount the remarks of the governor when he went on to say that Canada has been living beyond its means. No one will deny the problem presented by the inner six and the outer seven European nations. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) spoke of the apprehension felt by those countries who are concerned about the common market. Those member countries of the inner six and outer seven are also members of NATO. No one will question that Canada must trade or stagnate. Few will question that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) made fine representations on our behalf at the Paris conference.
The question I now ask, and I put it to the house, is this: Supposing this concern materializes and the inner six and outer seven set up a number of discriminatory trade barriers. Then we are in a position where our exports abroad will decline, and continue to decline, although, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out, and rightly so, they did increase in the last half of the year. We must then ask ourselves, what course of action do we now take?

There are only two possible courses to take, perhaps three. First, to impress upon the European communities that we assisted them when they needed assistance most; otherwise, continue to make representation. Second, we should perhaps examine the suggestion made by a senior official of the government of the United States who talked about closer trade relationship, in fact, a common market with Canada. Personally, I would have very serious reservations about this suggestion, because it would tie us even closer to the economy of the United States, even greater than we already are. Third, we have the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). He returned to this country from Europe, and he suggested that all levels, government, business, industry and labour, must work together to determine how best we can put ourselves in a competitive position to meet the new threat of competition from Europe.
This means, that business, for its part, cannot expect to have set up areas of tariff barriers protecting one industry when, on the other hand, we are expecting Europe to open up new areas. This means, in turn, that labour will have to reconcile its differences with management and also make some attempt to reduce costs. This means the government will have to pursue every possible channel to be absolutely certain we are diversifying all of the areas of trade, in the hope that we can develop new business.
Finally, I should like to introduce one other note with respect to the general economy of Canada. I spoke of the need for self discipline, because that is what it amounts to, as a means of competing with various countries which today are offering a new economic threat to us. Might I suggest that there is another area of self discipline in relation to our own economy in so far as it affects government and the people. Many hon. members may have read a report by a bank president commenting on interviews with some 19 young applicants for positions as junior clerks in a banking institution. Each of these young men concerned himself mainly, according to this report, with such questions as how soon he would be able to retire, the pension plan offered by the bank and the other social benefits which he would receive.
There is in this economy today no reason why we should not provide social benefits for the people of Canada as a whole, but I do suggest that the attitude of these 19 youngsters could symbolize something which amounts almost to an economic sickness which, if permitted' to continue, with its insistence that the state owes the individual a living. This will destroy personal incentive to such an extent that it will be difficult to
The Address-Mr. Cardin get people to do anything for themselves in any situation. I should make it clear that I do not believe we have reached this point yet, and it will be necessary, quite obviously, to maintain all the social services which we have come to accept; we may even have to increase some of them in order to assist those who live on fixed incomes.
But I suggest that some leadership could be given by the government and by industry in the hope that we can cut back this continued demand that the government must do everything. I intend this to apply not only to individuals but to business and industry which come down to Ottawa continually asking for increased assistance or to be bailed out of difficulty; requests which always require money from the treasury. I suggest that this government, which has shown courage beyond all belief in many fields-in establishing a commission to look at its own functions; in setting up committees of the house to determine the future of its own expenditures; in establishing methods by which we can develop the north; in establishing a foreign policy which has made the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) one of the great international leaders-this government could again make a contribution to Canada by encouraging and seeing that personal initiative is still recognized and that if you risk a dollar you are entitled to make a dollar in return. This is a worthy objective and one which will need the wholehearted co-operation not only of the government itself but of all the people within our dominion.

The attitude of the government makes it abundantly clear that the political philosophy the Conservatives adopted prior to 1957 of winning elections at any cost is still the basis of operation of the present administration and indeed it is the only explanation for the inconceivable discrepancies between government speeches and facts as they really are.
Just as the Conservatives did not hesitate to place before the Canadian public a host of ill-considered and impossible promises to

achieve power they do not now hesitate to hide their inefficiency, their irresponsibility and their incompetence behind a barrage of double talk and an avalanche of political propaganda and publicity stunts such as having the Prime Minister's picture taken with an angelic look in his eye and a halo over his head.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a comment at this point.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would do so later.

Such 'Grossartally' exaggerated publicity stunts could be considered humorous if it were not apparent from speeches of government members that they actually believe that because of his administration the Prime Minister deserves to be canonized. I think the members of the opposition will be forgiven for not sharing the blind and unjustified idolatry displayed by government members and for believing instead that it will take more than publicity and propaganda to meet the challenge of a rapidly evolving world and to earn the prosperity and stability that we hope will be Canada's fortune in the future.
At the last Progressive Conservative convention the order from the hierarchy was for Conservatives to get closer to the people. To my mind that is one tactic that will not enjoy any great success because everyone now knows that the closer the Conservatives get to the people the easier it will be for the government to put its hand in the taxpayers' pocket. And surely that is easy enough already. Income taxes are already too heavy, the cost of living is getting out of hand, interest rates are already too high and if the Conservatives get any closer they will smother the Canadian economy and the Canadian people as well.
It might be interesting to examine what the Conservatives mean when they talk about getting closer to the people. Were they being close to the people when they led them to believe that Conservatives would increase social security, reduce taxation and balance the budget, and ended up by increasing taxes and presenting a record deficit to the Canadian people? Was the Prime Minister close to the
The Address-Mr. Cardin people when he stated that not one Canadian would suffer from unemployment as long as he was Prime Minister and is he any closer now when he closes his eyes and his ears to the 722,000 unemployed in the country? Was he close to the provinces and municipalities when he shed so many crocodile tears over their financial plight and is he any closer now when he states that because of constitutional difficulties and federal obligations there is really nothing he can do about it?
Was the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) close to the Canadian people when he stated that it was not as important to tell the truth to the Canadian public during elections as it was to tell the truth in the House of Commons?
And in his speech in this very debate was the Prime Minister being close to the people? Three quarters of his speech was concentrated on attacking the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). He tortured the texts, he tortured himself and he tortured the house in a vain attempt to find substantial discrepancies in the statements of the Leader of the Opposition on defence policy and then illogically concluded that the Leader of the Opposition was following a sinuous and tortuous course.
Everyone knows that it is the tipsy driver who feels that the other fellow is not going straight and the Prime Minister's speeches from the time he took over leadership of his party to this day have been on countless occasions absolutely contradictory. The course followed by the Prime Minister is not only sinuous, it is sinister, as well.
For instance, in his speech the other day the Prime Minister, not having any real policy to offer on current issues and no answer or solution to present day urgent problems of defence and the high-cost economy, unemployment, and others, included in his speech the announcement of three important but surprise pieces of legislation the announcement of which would normally have been placed in the throne speech which was delivered just three or four days previously. The reason for this, of course, was to bolster up an otherwise completely empty speech and to detract public attention from the extremely serious difficulties and urgent problems that are challenging Canada's economic and military strength. In fact, the government has nothing to offer. ,
The sinister part of the Prime Minister's course is that the Prime Minister himself is attempting to lull Canadians into a false sense of security and a most unrealistic approach to the future when he should be extremely active and anxious to inform the people of the dangers and pitfalls that now stand in Canada's path.
