The Address-Mr. Cardin
I do not consider that my remarks are pessimistic. There is no pessimism on this side of the house as to Canada's future but there is a profound realization of the existence of problems which must be solved before Canada's future can be considered assured. There are certain signs in our economy which force us to ask just how the Canadian economy will fit into the broad and rapidly shifting picture of international trade.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made a report recently on the Paris meeting and the developments taking place in the common market and the free trade area. He explained how Canada has now become a member of OAEC, and certainly these are all steps in the right direction for international trade.
I feel, however, that Canada should take an inward look and see just how well prepared Canada is to compete in world markets where there is a definite tendency toward freer trade and greater competition. It would appear as though Canada has already reached the stage-I am not speaking now of dumping or unfair competition-where fair competition from abroad has seriously cut into our home markets and in certain cases has jeopardized important industries. The textile industry, our merchant marine and the shipbuilding industry are obvious examples but there are others and there will be more if the problem is not soon solved.
I do not have to describe the plight of the textile industry. Suffice it to say that one after the other textile mills are being closed. Nor do I need to stress how ridiculous and, indeed, how unacceptable it is for Canada, whose economy depends more and more on exports and whose very slogan is from sea to sea, to have not one ship under Canadian registry at either its eastern or western ports and, indeed, for the government of Canada to sell its last few remaining ships because it could not operate them economically.
How many did your government sell?

Then, of course, there is the closely related shipbuilding industry which at this time should be increasingly active and flourishing but which is actually grinding to a standstill in spite of the fact that our shipyards are well and modernly equipped and that our technicians and skilled labour are second to none in the world. There is something fundamentally wrong when hundreds and thousands of shipyard workers in my home town and in shipyards throughout the country have to sit back and watch Canada's export trade being carried by foreign ships while our shipyard workers 

and our sailors are trying to live on unemployment insurance. I read recently that even our Canadian steel industries are beginning to find importation of foreign steel a little disconcerting and are beginning to suggest that we should raise trade barriers against the importation of steel.
The point I wish to make here is that if a growing number of Canadian industries are continually losing a good part of our own home markets to foreign competition to the point of having to abandon activity in these fields in some cases, what will Canada's chances be in the future in selling its products in a more competitive world market? If Mr. Khrushchev does launch an all-out economic war, as he has threatened to do, just how well is Canada prepared to meet the unrealistic and drastic price structure involved in such an attack? If Canada cannot meet this extreme situation and, indeed, if it cannot meet the price structure of extended freer trade and greater competition, what will happen to the Canadian economy?
In presenting his report of the international trade meeting in Paris the other day the minister presented what to my mind was only half of a very important problem. I am not sure which half of the problem is more important but the other half of the problem to which the minister did not refer is to find out exactly how we are going to make Canadian prices competitive in this era of freer trade and greater competition. I do not believe anyone will dispute the wisdom of freer trade under present conditions but that, of course, does not make the Canadian problem of high prices any easier.
What is the answer? I would be more than a genius, Mr. Speaker, if I had the answer to that problem and I would be more than a fool if I pretended that either the cause or the solution were simple. But one thing is sure, that it is unpardonable irresponsibility on the part of the government to act as though the problem did not exist, and it is economic suicide for the government to let the people believe that Canada can achieve economic stability and true prosperity without having solved it.
I realize that this subject is a really hot potato but I honestly believe that it is one that can no longer be ignored by the house or by the people, no matter how hot it is. I believe that our whole parliamentary system and this house in particular were created in order to recognize, to study and to try to solve, if possible, all national problems, certainly those as fundamental and as vital as this one.
It is preposterous for a government to close its eyes to the real problems because of their

difficulty and to concentrate its attention on certain legislation because of its popularity. Certainly it will be a fine thing to have a bill of rights but I wonder just how much comfort it will be to Canadians to read about freedoms, liberties and rights they have always possessed if the bottom falls out of the Canadian economy?
Surely the government cannot possibly and will not refuse the invitation extended to it by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress to attend a meeting of government, labour and management. I am sure that the government can usefully use this opportunity offered to it in order to make a thoroughly objective and exhaustive study into the general causes of and possible solutions to our high cost economy. Also, Mr. Speaker, in this meeting the problems that are now facing those industries whose very existence is jeopardized by foreign competition might well be studied. I do not feel that the solution to the problem of these affected industries will be found among the traditionally accepted solutions of the past, high tariffs, quotas and restrictions which, to my mind, under present economic trends will become as obsolete as economic isolationism itself.
To find a solution to the problem we will have to be far more imaginative and be bolder than we have ever been. We will have to explore other vistas of our free enterprise system and tap other sources of initiative, energy and strength from both labour and management who together have made Canada the industrial power it now is. Although there are many other causes of our high cost economy, I would be less than truthful if I did not say that I believe that the persistent and apparently irreconcilable differences in the points of view of these two giants of industry, labour and management, have been rocking Canada's economic boat. I do not believe it is in the interests of either labour or management or Canadians generally that we should let the boat capsize regardless of who is right and who is wrong.
Nor do I believe that the responsibility for the present difficulties can be placed on labour any more than on management. The blame might well be put on the origin or the circumstances under which the relationship between labour and management was founded centuries ago, a relationship of lord and vassal which is of course no longer compatible under our progressive social standards and reforms and, indeed, not accepted by either labour or management. But even after many generations there still exists between labour and management the same diametrically opposed interests and points of
The Address-Mr. Cardin view of feudal days. These differences can only widen with increasing competition which we now foresee.
If we could find a new basis or a new principle on which to found, not a relationship but a veritable partnership between these two giants, I believe that we would have gone a long way toward solving our problem of a high cost economy and the Canadian economy itself would be in a far stronger position to meet any challenge the world would have to offer. Many informed people in Canada have spoken of the desirability of having more Canadians invest more money in Canadian industry. I fully agree with that principle. Industry itself could, and perhaps should, encourage and facilitate the investment of capital by their employees in the industry or plant where the majority of these employees spend the greater part of their lives and to which they have contributed so much.
The government also might, in a very tangible way, encourage employees to invest in the industry or plant in which they work. If we look at what is being done in other fields of our economic activity, income tax deductions, government guaranteed loans earmarked for certain purposes could no longer be considered to be too revolutionary. This type of participation in benefits is already being followed by several companies in Canada with considerable success, and a comparable partnership of labour and management might be usefully adopted in a far greater number of industries. I am not at all sure that the industries most affected by foreign competition, which we must keep alive, might not find in this way the new energy, the new strength, the new power that is necessary to make them viable, once labour and management are both pulling in the same direction and toward the same objective.
The return of capital to the original investors-because for many reasons even the employees' participation in the new partnership should be in dollars and cents-could usefully be reinvested in the purchase of more modern machinery or might be reinvested in other industries. The employees, on the other hand, would have a sense of belonging which they have never had before and which would spark interest in their work which would translate itself into increased production and a reduction of costs. Employee participation in profits, along with their salaries, would give them a greater annual revenue, and their shares in the company would give them a sort of built-in pension plan. It seems to me that from this

The Address-Mr. J. Smith partnership there could arise a great number of social benefits which are of importance.
The employees, on the other hand, would have a greater appreciation of the possibilities of the industry and understand the difficulties being met by the industry by having representatives on the board of directors, by having reports from the company and watching the balance sheet. I am convinced that the employees could and would find appropriate solutions to the problems of management which management might never be able to find alone. Mr. Speaker, whether we follow this method or not I cannot help but think that the farther we get away from this lord-vassal type of relationship between labour and management, whose respective interests are, by their very nature, diametrically opposed to one another and the oloser we can come to a partnership of these two essential halves of industry where the interest of one is also the interest of the other, then the oloser we will be to solving the problems of our high-cost economy, and stabilizing our industries without sacrificing Canada's high standard of living.
I would strongly urge the government to accept the invitation of the labour congress and even to attempt a field experiment in the textile, ship-operating and shipbuilding industries, under the sponsorship of government, of labour, of management, of technicians and economists, in a combined effort to try to save these vital industries, and with a view to exploring the limitless possibilities to be found in the free enterprise system and in the will and determination of the Canadian people to make of Canada the truly great nation it can become. It is this government's most sacred responsibility to give to the country the leadership and the guidance necessary to attain that end. We on this side respectfully submit that this government has not assumed that responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity that I have had to speak in this house during the throne speech debate. I welcome this opportunity and, like other hon. members, I am going to limit my remarks to matters pertaining to the county which I represent. I will, on behalf of that county, give some credit to this government for the many things they have done. I hope, also, I shall make some suggestions which will be useful.
I extend to you, sir, my congratulations on being appointed Deputy Speaker of this house. I extend congratulations also to the Sergeant-at-Arms. To Mr. Franklin, who has just retired, I convey my wishes for a long and happy retired life. I should like also to extend to the mover (Mr. Morissette) and seconder

(Mrs. Casselman) of the speech from the throne my sincere congratulations for a job which was exceptionally well done.
The riding which I represent, Lincoln county, being part of the Niagara peninsula is steeped in the history and tradition of the early days when Upper Canada was first settled by the Anglo-Saxon people. The first government of Upper Canada was held at Niagara-on-the-Lake in Lincoln county. The part played by General Isaac Brock, Laura Secord and Butler's Bangers during the war of 1812 and at the battle of Queenston Heights is proudly remembered by the people of the Niagara peninsula and, I am sure, by the people of Canada. Sometimes I think that our government here in Ottawa could do more from the national standpoint to preserve the heritage and traditions of these early settlers, the British colonial soldiers, and the part they played in defending the boundary line between Canada and the United States along the banks of the Niagara river.
Old Fort Mississagua, which stands at the mouth of the Niagara river across from old Fort Niagara, which is on the United States side, is deteriorating fast. In order that it be preserved for the future repair work will have to be done soon or the old building will become a complete ruin. At the present time the roof is still intact. I believe this fort was built about the same time as Fort Henry at Kingston. There are other old buildings at Niagara-on-the-Lake, such as the old St. Mark's Anglican church, the old St. Andrew's Presbyterian church, which are gems of early Canadian architecture, some of them dating back prior to the burning of old Niagara during the war of 1812.
Those old buildings are really buildings that should be preserved for all time. The old St. Andrew's church intrigues me. The box stalls where the family sit together, with the little door that you fasten with a bolt when you go in; the high pulpit with the winding stair going up either side; and the padded sounding board extending over the minister's desk could be Scotland's contribution to early acoustics.
The Ontario provincial government have done an excellent job in restoring and preserving Fort George navy hall, the Mac-Farlane house, Queenston Heights and many other historial places all along the Niagara river to Fort Erie. That is so from a provincial standpoint. However, I do feel that since Niagara-on-the-Lake was the cradle of constituted government in Upper Canada from a national standpoint it deserves a little bit more prominence and a little bit more money being spent on preserving what is left of those early colonial days.

I am concerned about old Fort Mississagua and have brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) who has advised me that he will send one of his department officials to Niagara-on-the-Lake this spring to inspect the old fort in conjunction with officials of the Niagara parks commission.
Those early settlers who came to Niagara peninsula were United Empire Loyalists. They came to Canada after the war of independence in the United States and they brought with them their tools and experience in farming and milling which gave them a good start and so the Niagara area developed fast in those early days.
The scriptures tell us that when the Israelites left Egypt and journeyed into the promised land they carried with them little fig trees and seeds of corn. I am sure those early settlers coming into the Niagara peninsula across the treacherous Niagara river in the Conestoga wagons may have brought with them little peach trees and grapevines as well as their other belongings.
Fruit and vegetable growing is the Niagara peninsula's oldest industry and still is the most important one. However, I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that over the past 20 years when the former government was in power the problems of the growers were sadly neglected. Each year their markets were flooded with surplus and subsidized crops from the United States dumped into Canada just at a time when the Niagara crops were ready to harvest. This procedure had a very discouraging effect on the fruit growers and during those years many of the old family farms were broken up and sold into small acreages for week-end farmers, housing subdivisions and industrial sites and many of the young people left the farms.
However, I do not agree with some of the writings in our newspaper about the fruit growing industry in the Niagara peninsula being finished or nearly finished. It is true that those years of indifference to the growers by the former government have damaged the industry and it will take some time to correct that damage.
We still have plenty of the good land, the good climate and the know-how to grow good fruit; and if the growers continue to receive the same sympathetic support that our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) is giving them now there will be delicious peaches from the Niagara peninsula for a long time to come. However, long range planning of the fruit lands is essential and growers must be assured of a fair share of the Canadian market.
The Address-Mr. J. Smith
Those fruit growers do not want high tariffs or unreasonable legislation. All they want is protection against the dumping of surplus crops from the United States into Canada at times when Canadian crops are ready to harvest. Government assistance to recover the British market for canned fruit which was also lost by the former government is also essential. It is extremely interesting to note today that there is going to be some change in the dollar situation, something which might help us to sell more of our canned fruit in the United Kingdom.
During the 1957 election the growers asked for three items of legistation, namely a seasonal tariff during the harvesting season, fair value for duty purposes and price stabilization. These items were all designed to combat dumping from the United States. Those acts are now all in effect except a section of Bill No. C-51 which has not been proclaimed so far. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) announced that fruit and vegetables were Canada's third highest import from the United States. Surely fair value for duty to protect our market during the harvesting season from dumping by United States growers would be in order.
The outlook of the Niagara fruit industry has substantially improved in the last two years and most of the growers report good returns for 1959, except some growers who suffered considerable crop damage by hailstorm and wind. Those growers are considering this new crop insurance act very seriously.
The uncertainty of the canning industry, as the result of a great many of the Canadian canning factories having been bought up by United States interests and many having been closed down is causing much concern among the growers.
The passing of the small corner grocery store trade and the apparent end of home canning-which together provided a market for about 40 per cent of the basket crop- is also a problem that is gradually being overcome. This basket fruit business is moving into the hands of the big chain stores who buy in large quantities, thus making it necessary for the growers to form collective marketing agencies with suitable cold storage facilities so as to hold the crop in storage when necessary awaiting shipment.
There is a great need for improved marketing facilities with good cold storage facilities in the Niagara peninsula and grants by the federal government which are available now to build cold storage plants should be encouraged so that more companies will take advantage of those plants to improve their storage facilities.

The Address-Mr. J. Smith
There is not too much mixed farming in my riding and time will not permit that I deal with it at this time. However, at some time in the future, during the estimates, I hope to deal with it.
Building and operating of ship canals has always played an important part in the every day life of the people of Lincoln county. Three canals have been built across the Niagara peninsula. The first started construction soon after the war of 1812 and was completed in 1829.
I must say a word about this old canal. It is very important at this time because for 20 years the people of the Niagara peninsula asked and begged the former government to do something about cleaning it up and restoring the canal lands to their original state, but did not obtain satisfactory results. The then department of transport did make several unrealistic cash offers that the municipalities do the clean-up job themselves, which was entirely impossible. So it fell to our present Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to find the money and proceed with the job, which is now well under way. Some of my good Liberal friends, and my friends in the C.C.F. too, who supported me in the last two elections say it was well worth switching their votes to get the old canal cleaned up; and so it was, because children were often drowned in the unguarded muddy water, and it was an ugly eyesore to the whole community.
The hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) in her eloquent speech referred to empty cargo vessels passing down the seaway. Well, we have that too. We also have it in another way in the Niagara peninsula-miles of freight trains come loaded across the international bridges at Niagara Falls and Fort Erie and return empty to the United States. This is too much of a one-way business for the good of Canada. This is the result of our imbalance of trade with the United States which was fostered by the trade policies and GATT arrangements of the former government, which reached an all-time high in 1956.
Our former government seemed afraid of retaliation by the United States government. I do not see things that way. Neither do I believe in sudden changes, but rather a gradual equalization of our tariff regulations on farm products and manufactured goods entering the United States or Canada. It is necessary at least to be on an equal footing. If there is a 25 per cent duty on a Canadian product entering the United States, then it should be the same on a United States product entering Canada unless, of course, the product is citrus fruit or fresh fruit out of season, or other food products we cannot grow in

Canada, or products we cannot manufacture in Canada. In this case tariffs are not necessary.
Far be it from me to be an economist, but it does appear to me that Canada would be better off if our currency rates with the United States were also equalized.
The slump in Canada's textile manufacturing industry has been felt in Lincoln county. Over the past 20 years we have lost several fine industries. Statistics tell us that some 15 years ago Canada's textile industry was Canada's highest employer of labour, but now it has dropped to less than the third highest. This should be of concern to all Canadians, and I for one repudiate a statement often heard that Canada should not be in the textile industry at all, that we cannot compete, and that business should go elsewhere.
Two world wars have shown us that we can be isolated, and we need to keep all our industries. While I am not a believer in high tariffs I do favour quotas, which seem to me to be the only way we can save what is left of our once prosperous textile industry. The same set of facts applies to other light industry such as small tools and hardware.
Regarding the sale of our wheat and the threat of Russia planting millions more acres of wheat, that matter is very disturbing. Sometimes I wonder if we are putting enough research and study into ways and means of selling or processing some of our wheat into a food product that would be more acceptable to backward countries of the world that are in need of food, countries that may not have the facilities for processing wheat themselves.
We hear much from certain people about tight money. When I look around my riding and other parts of Canada I see evidence of national development on a broad scale. In Ontario the provincial government is spending millions on much needed highways and other public projects. Schools, houses, sewer and water projects are being built and installed at a fast pace by all the municipalities.
There may be a slowing down of credit on second-class risks due to the demand for capital being greater than the supply, but there certainly is no sign of a decline in the general construction industry, either by private enterprise, by governments or by municipalities. Perhaps the land of my origin where money is always tight makes me immune to the lament about tight money coming from the other side of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I find in my own riding that people who are being displaced by automation in some of our heavy industries, and the decline of the textile and other light industry due to foreign imports, are finding it difficult to be absorbed into other industry,

especially those past middle age. This is a matter the government should take under advisement.
However, the people of Lincoln county do appreciate the things this government has promised and done. Price stabilization on the peach crop last year avoided what looked like a complete loss to many of the growers when the canning industry slumped and there was the old threat of dumping from the United States. Price stabilization went into effect on the peach crop with good results to the growers.
The clean-up of the old Welland ship canal after so many years of passing the buck, as it were, by the former government is something which our people are very pleased about. We appreciate what the Department of Transport has done in helping to develop a regional airport in the Niagara peninsula and the improvements now under way on the seaway Welland ship canal.
I trust that matters pertaining to pilots on the Port Weller-Sarnia part of the seaway will be settled to the satisfaction of the Canadian and United States authorities and the pilots before navigation opens; also that a civil service competition for the position of supervisor of pilots will be called, and that that matter, which has been a very contentious one, will also be settled before navigation opens.
I have suggested to the Minister of Transport that consideration might soon be given to improved facilities for salvage and rescue on the great lakes and the seaway. I feel that Canada should have a first-class salvage and rescue ship on each of the great lakes capable of providing fire protection, towing and general rescue work. I think we rely too much on the United States coastguard service on the great lakes and with the opening of the seaway and the increased water transportation we might well be thinking of a Canadian coastguard service of our own.
The opening up of the seaway is also bringing new business to Lincoln county. Our shipyard at Port Weller has been successful in securing a contract to build a new deep sea passenger and freight vessel for the British West India trade. Bauxite which at one time came to the abrasive industries in Niagara peninsula by United States railway lines is now coming by deep sea vessels through the seaway and a local company is spending a substantial sum of money building new wharfage facilities for unloading large ocean freighters bringing bauxite and other raw materials to some of our local industries. The very large number of tourists who visited the seaway Welland ship canal last summer gives promise of an increased tourist attraction to the canal area and in conjunction
Division
with historic old Niagara and Niagara Falls I see a greater tourist industry awaiting further development.
The matter of tolls on the Welland ship canal is causing deep concern to industries in the Hamilton-Niagara peninsula area who bring to this area Canadian raw materials such as pulpwood, coal and iron ore to be processed, and ship out such products as paper, steel and package freight, destined to points in the United States and various parts of Canada.

subtopic: DEBT CHARGES
DEBT CHARGES
speechtext:
1.	Has St. Paul's hospital, Saskatoon, or anybody acting on its behalf, advised the government that it will be necessary to close the hospital unless government assistance is obtained in financing capital debt?
2.	Has the government received representations from St. Paul's hospital, Saskatoon, or anybody acting on its behalf, requesting the federal government to include interest charges on capital debt in its payments on account of the hospital insurance act?
3.	If so, what reply has been made by the government to such representations?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monleith (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	No.
2.	and 3. Representations were received from the minister of public health in Saskatchewan requesting that consideration be given to modifying the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act so as to include certain capital costs. It was stated that the matter was of importance in connection with construction programs, particularly the St. Paul's hospital in Saskatoon.
The full text of the reply from the Minister of National Health and Welfare dated August 20, 1959, is as follows:
"Dear Mr. Erb:
Thank you for your letter of August 12 concerning the possibility of modifying the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to permit the inclusion of depreciation on physical plant and interest on money borrowed for capital purposes.
At the time the act was drafted, amounts expended on the capital cost of land, buildings and physical plant, depreciation thereon and amounts expended for the payment of any capital debt or interest thereon were excluded from the operation of the act after very careful consideration.
In the last few months, the inclusion of some or all of the items has been urged from time to time, and further careful consideration has been given to the issues involved. It may be said, I feel, that opinion regarding both the desirability and the means of including these items is not unanimous, and that, furthermore, their inclusion would raise extremely difficult problems.
The hospital insurance program is a new and expanding one, and while undoubtedly
Questions
careful and continuing review of the situation is essential, I am of the opinion that radical changes or modifications should only be made in the light of further experience gained through the operation of the program.
In view of this, I regret that I am not in a position to make an announcement concerning these matters at the present time.
Yours sincerely,
J. Waldo Monteith.
The Honourable J. Walter Erb,
Minister of Public Health,
Provincial Health Building,
Regina, Saskatchewan."

ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY  MEETINGS RESPECTING CONTRACT 49
speechtext:
1.	Have any meetings been held between contractors or their representatives, and officials of the St. Lawrence seaway authority or the Department of Transport, for the purpose of discussing (a) work completed under contract number 49;	(b)
or payment thereof?
2.	If so, (a) what was the date of each; (b) where were they held; (c) what officials attended each;
(d)	what was the nature of the discussions; (e) what decisions were reached; (f) which decisions were carried out, and on what date?
3.	Has the St. Lawrence seaway authority or the Department of Transport obtained legal advice regarding payment on this contract?
4.	If so, (a) what official did so; (b) on what date; (c) nature of request; (d) what advice was received; (e) what legal counsel was approached; (f) what action was taken?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minisier of Transpori):
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises as follows:
1. Regular meetings were held throughout the period of execution of the work between the contractor's engineers and representatives and the engineers of the authority. Prior to completion of the work, a claim was submitted by the contractor to the authority. With a view to negotiating a settlement of the claim, meetings were held between the engineers or the chief engineer of the authority and the engineers of the contractor. Meetings were also held and discussions took place relative to the legal aspects of the claim between counsel for the contractor and counsel for the authority. Further meetings were held between respresentatives of the contractor and authority, with counsel

for the contractor and counsel for the authority in attendance. No settlement has yet been reached.
2, 3, 4. Answered by Question 1.

speechtext:
1. Have officials of the St. Lawrence seaway authority accepted each individual set of gates and associated machinery of each individual lock as a completed working unit, according to plans and specifications at the St. Lawrence seaway authority?
2.	If so, what official of the authority has done so in each case, what was the date of acceptance, the name of the official signing, and was it with his personal knowledge? If not, the name of officials recommending acceptance, and the positions held by same?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minisier of
Transport):
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises as follows:
1.	Separate contracts were given for supply and erection of gates, for the operation mechanisms and for the electrical systems. Subject to the warranty stipulated in the contract, the work under each contract is accepted individually when the chief engineer, in writing, certifies to final completion in accordance with the plans and specifications. In giving such certificate, the chief engineer relies not only on his personal knowledge, but on the reports of his senior engineer assistants.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
